tldr: We introduce the Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS), where a humanoid robot braces against a wall with one hand to support itself. Without human motion data or online trajectory planning, the robot achieves sustained contact forces up to 60 N.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS). A support configuration covering the entire task region is pre-optimised offline. Two synchronous policies—one for the lower body, torso, and supporting arm, and another for the working arm—run simultaneously. This dissipates strong reaction forces while achieving stable end-effector trajectory and force tracking.
overview:
Unlike industrial robot arms bolted to the floor, bipedal humanoids are fixed to the environment only through their feet. As a result, when performing contact tasks like cutting, polishing, or forceful pushing, the large reaction forces at the end-effector travel through the whole body, easily breaking balance.

When humans need to exert large forces, they instinctively lean on a nearby wall or table with one hand to brace themselves. Inspired by this behaviour, this work develops the Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS). A humanoid braces against the environment with one hand while executing forceful manipulation with the other. Crucially, offline optimisation finds a single, optimal support configuration for the entire task region. This configuration serves as a geometric guide for two synchronous reinforcement-learning (RL) policies: a body policy (torso and supporting arm) and a working arm policy. The approach requires no online whole-body trajectory planning, no human demonstrations, and not even runtime force sensor feedback.

In real-robot experiments on a Unitree G1, an unbraced baseline sustained only 13.5 N, whereas SHS achieved usable contact forces up to 60 N. Furthermore, conditioning the support configuration on the task region substantially improved trajectory and force tracking. The system also generalised immediately to different task regions without retraining the policies.
contributions: Proposed SHS, the first strategy for floating-base humanoids that uses one hand for environmental bracing to enhance the forceful manipulation capability of the other hand.
Developed a framework (TRSO and WBKR) that optimises a single support configuration offline to cover an entire task region, without human demonstrations or online trajectory generation.

Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 a major expansion in force capacity (up to 60 N compared to 13.5 N unbraced), high-precision trajectory and force tracking, and zero-shot transfer across task regions without retraining.

sections.heading: Bracing against a wall lets robots exert much more force
sections.summary: When humanoids perform heavy tasks, reaction forces sway the base and break balance. Just like humans brace with one hand, this work introduces SHS to expand whole-body force generation using environmental support.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots, forceful contact tasks such as cutting, polishing, and pushing remain extremely difficult. Unlike manipulators bolted to the floor, humanoids have a floating base. Reaction forces generated at the end-effector propagate through the kinematic chain across the entire body, destabilising posture.

Humans naturally brace against a wall or table with one hand when pushing or polishing heavy objects. This extra contact mechanically supports the body and counteracts the reaction forces felt by the working hand. This paper proposes the Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS) to bring this principle to humanoids.

The core idea of SHS is not to mimic human motion capture data, but to compute mechanically how to brace stably. A single support configuration satisfying the requirements of the entire task region is optimised offline. It then guides two RL policies: a body policy and a working arm policy. This practical approach operates without runtime force sensor feedback and without online whole-body trajectory generation.

sections.heading: Bridging the gap between multi-contact control and RL
sections.summary: Conventional multi-contact control relies heavily on models and sensors, while RL methods often depend on demonstrations or online trajectory generation. This method takes a new approach by deriving a region-wide support configuration offline without demonstrations.
sections.details:
Environmental bracing has long been studied in fixed-base robots to prevent arm deflection and reduce energy consumption. Many studies also explore multi-contact balancing and contact force control for humanoids. However, conventional model-based control demands precise full-body dynamic models and rich contact sensing, posing high hurdles for real-world deployment.

On the other hand, recent RL-based humanoid controllers adapt well to disturbances and contacts, but none have formulated environmental bracing as a task-level mechanism to amplify working force. Furthermore, common RL approaches rely on human demonstrations (retargeting) or online generation of dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories to follow.

To address this, the authors chose to optimise a single support configuration offline that covers the whole task region, using it as a geometric reference to guide the RL policies. This enables robust environmental bracing and forceful manipulation without human demonstrations, online trajectory generation, or force sensor feedback.

captions.F2: The overall SHS pipeline: (a) define task and support regions, (b, c) optimise a single support configuration via TRSO for the entire region, (d) represent skeletal keypoints in a pelvis-relative frame (WBKR), and (e) provide them as reference targets to two synchronous RL policies controlling the body/supporting arm and the working arm.

sections.heading: How offline support optimisation and synchronous dual policies work
sections.summary: SHS consists of three elements: Task-Region Support Optimisation (TRSO), Whole-Body Keypoint Representation (WBKR), and synchronous dual policies. It covers the entire region with a single support posture while maintaining stable control without end-effector force feedback.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Task-Region Support Optimisation (TRSO)
TRSO finds a single support configuration offline that satisfies end-effector positions and normal force requirements (0 to 75 N) across the task region, while honouring static balance and joint limits. The optimisation variables comprise a 14-dimensional support configuration $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{s}}$ shared across the region (foot-midpoint position, ankle/pelvis pitch, waist joints, supporting arm joints) and 8-dimensional per-sample variables (working arm joints and supporting hand normal force). Using Sequential Least Squares Quadratic Programming (SLSQP), it minimises a penalty function accounting for contact surface alignment, end-effector tracking, friction cone constraints, and Zero Moment Point (ZMP) margins inside the support polygon. Rather than re-planning the full trajectory online, one posture covers the entire task region.

### III-C Whole-Body Keypoint Representation (WBKR)
WBKR converts the optimised posture into geometric references that policies can easily track. It uses 21 dimensions: vector $\mathbf{s}$ from the foot midpoint to the pelvis, and relative vectors $\mathbf{r}_j$ from the pelvis to key body points (chest, both shoulders, both elbows, supporting hand). Defining positions relative to the pelvis ensures that leg tracking errors do not directly alter upper-body posture targets.

### III-D Synchronous Dual RL Policies
Control is split between two policies. The working arm policy $\pi_{\mathrm{w}}$ controls the 7 working arm joints, while the body policy $\pi_{\mathrm{b}}$ controls the 22 joints across both legs, the waist, and the supporting arm. Rather than a hierarchical setup, both run synchronously using a shared 143-dimensional observation. Notably, the policy inputs include no force sensor measurements. Contact forces are modulated indirectly through proprioception alone (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.). Training proceeds in two stages: training on static targets (Stage 1), followed by dynamic trajectory tracking with the body policy frozen (Stage 2). Drawing from real-world hardware observations where shoulder pitch actuators overheated, the reward includes a quartic torque utilisation penalty that heavily punishes highly stressed joints.

sections.heading: What makes it work? Rigorous real-world and simulation testing
sections.summary: Using a real Unitree G1 and simulation, experiments were designed to isolate the effects of environmental bracing, geometric references, and task-conditioned optimisation, comparing against unbraced baselines.
sections.details:
### IV-A Baselines and Ablations
To evaluate the proposed method, the authors tested the following setups:
- **SHS**: The proposed method referencing an optimised, task-conditioned support configuration (WBKR).
- **Generic**: References a single representative posture (dataset median) shared across all task regions.
- **No-reference**: An ablation removing the support configuration reference, attempting to brace purely through contact rewards.
- **No-bracing**: An ablation with no supporting hand, performing tasks solely by leaning the body forward.
- **Modular**: A standard unbraced baseline combining the robot's built-in lower-body RL controller with working-arm inverse kinematics (IK) and a force control loop.

### IV-B & IV-C Evaluation Protocol and Hardware Setup
The real-world robot was a 29-DoF Unitree G1 equipped with a 6-axis force/torque sensor (ATI Axia80-M20) at the working wrist for evaluation (the RL policies do not use this sensor for control).
Two experiments were conducted:
1. **Fixed-position force capacity (Experiment 1)**: With the end-effector held at a fixed position, target normal force stepped from 0 to 80 N in 10 N increments to evaluate the maximum sustainable force.
2. **Trajectory tracking performance (Experiment 2)**: Tracing a figure-8 trajectory on a vertical surface under 10 to 70 N of force, measuring path and force RMS errors. Additionally, task regions shifted by 5 cm horizontally and vertically (T2, T3) tested whether the system adapts simply by re-optimising the support posture without retraining the policies.

sections.heading: From 13.5 N unbraced to 60 N! Massive force gains and smooth tracking
sections.summary: SHS achieved up to 60 N of sustained contact force, far exceeding the 13.5 N of the unbraced baseline. Task-conditioned support postures sharply reduced trajectory and force tracking errors, and zero-shot transfer succeeded without retraining.
sections.details:
### V-A Force Range Expansion via Environmental Bracing
In Experiment 1, the unbraced Modular baseline could only sustain at most 13.5 N for 1 second, with a practical usable force of about 10 N. In contrast, SHS sustained up to 60 N at middle and upper positions, and 40 N at lower positions (Generic reached 40 to 50 N). In simulation, the No-bracing ablation revealed an interesting failure mode: because it leaned its body forward, body weight rested on the end-effector, preventing it from exerting low forces (minimum force stayed above 21 N). Environmental bracing is essential to cover the full force continuum from low to high loads.

### V-B & V-C Tracking Precision from Task-Conditioned Optimisation
In Experiment 2's figure-8 tracking under a 55 N load, SHS reduced force RMS error from 13.1 N to 9.2 N (a 30% reduction) and position RMS error from 5.1 cm to 3.6 cm (a 29% reduction) compared to Generic. Modular lost contact and failed above 11 N. Under high loads (40 to 70 N), SHS reduced working-shoulder wobble by a factor of 2.7 to 3.8 compared to Generic. Optimising the support configuration for the task stabilises the base of the working arm, leading directly to higher tracking accuracy.

### V-D Zero-Shot Transfer Without Retraining
For shifted task regions T2 (horizontal offset) and T3 (vertical offset), only the support configurations were recomputed via TRSO and fed into the frozen policies. Across 10 to 55 N, the system maintained tracking performance comparable to T1 (force RMS error 5.2 to 6.2 N, position RMS error 2.8 to 3.4 cm). This confirms the practical utility of flexibly shifting task spaces without additional policy training.

captions.F5: Comparison of figure-8 trajectory tracking at 55 N on the real robot: (a) proposed SHS versus (b) Generic with a representative posture. SHS stays much closer to the target path (black line) while maintaining stable normal force (colour-coded).

sections.heading: Why bracing works, and questions that remain
sections.summary: Environmental bracing overcomes both the 'standing upright cannot exert force' barrier and the 'leaning forward cannot unload' barrier. However, requiring the arm to reach the entire region from a single posture and expanding beyond planar contact remain open challenges.
sections.details:
Unbraced baselines run into two opposing failure modes. Staying upright (Modular) yields a low force ceiling because the robot cannot resist large reaction forces. Leaning forward (No-bracing) yields a high force floor because body weight rests on the tool, making delicate low-force tasks impossible. Bracing a hand against a wall is an exceptionally rational mechanism that eliminates both constraints simultaneously.

Another compelling insight is that optimising the support configuration for the task region provides natural mechanical stiffness and joint range margin at the shoulder. This enables stable force control without needing end-effector force sensors.

As a limitation, the method assumes the working arm can reach the entire task region from a single support posture. Extremely large workspaces would require repositioning the supporting hand. Furthermore, this study only evaluated contact against flat, vertical walls. Extending the framework to tensile supports, such as grasping poles or hooking onto handrails, remains future work.

sections.heading: A simple hand on the wall unlocks far stronger robots
sections.summary: This study introduced SHS, bracing against the environment with one hand to perform forceful manipulation with the other. Demonstrating up to 60 N of contact force on a real humanoid highlights the immense power of actively using the environment for support.
sections.details: For floating-base humanoids, intentionally using environmental bracing through SHS is a simple yet powerful framework that dramatically boosts heavy-duty manipulation without complex online trajectory generation or human demonstrations. On a real Unitree G1, it expanded sustained contact force from 13.5 N unbraced to 60 N, while task-conditioned posture optimisation substantially improved trajectory and force tracking. These results offer practical and valuable insights for deploying humanoids as functional tools in real-world heavy-work environments.

takeaways: Adopting the simple human behaviour of bracing against a wall quadruples a humanoid's sustainable contact force (13.5 N to 60 N).
Pre-computing a single static optimal support posture for an entire task region provides ample workspace reach and stability without re-planning whole-body trajectories online.
Precise force tracking is achievable without runtime end-effector force feedback, relying solely on appropriate support geometry and RL proprioception.
Simply updating the reference support configuration allows zero-shot adaptation to new task regions without retraining policies.
limitations: Limited to task regions reachable by the working arm from a single support configuration; larger workspaces would require repositioning the supporting hand.
Restricted to flat vertical wall contacts (compression and friction only); tensile supports such as grasping handrails remain untested.
Support posture optimisation (TRSO) relies on local optimisation via non-linear programming (SLSQP).
